column5: The course says the Arusha Declaration of 05/02/1967 'proclaimed ujamaa, familyhood, an African socialism of self-reliance, nationalisation and villages'. The text itself never uses the word ujamaa and does not mention villagisation or compulsory villages; it sets out the TANU creed, a policy of socialism (the major means of production, including banks, insurance, trade and big factories, to be controlled by peasants and workers through the government and co-operatives), a policy of self-reliance and a leadership code. It names no nationalisations (it says some means 'are already owned or controlled' by the government). The villagisation of 1973 to 1976 came later and is not in this text. The date 05/02/1967 is the declaration's date; the National Executive Committee met at Arusha 26/01/1967 to 29/01/1967 per its resolution. Rewrite the sentence: socialism and self-reliance, a leadership code, emphasis on agriculture; ujamaa and villages come from related documents and later policy.

column4: Leadership code and critique of urban bias
column5: Part Five bars TANU and government leaders from holding company shares or private directorships, drawing two or more salaries, or renting out houses, and defines 'leader' to include ministers, MPs, senior civil servants and a spouse. Nyerere also warns that town dwellers can exploit peasants because loans spent in towns are repaid from the farmers' export earnings. Primary evidence for the 'aim' side of the course's 'did ujamaa fail?' table; outcomes need other sources. Population quoted: 'more than ten million' (1967) and about 362,000 square miles.

column4: Self-reliance against aid, gifts, loans and foreign investment
column5: Part Three argues that Tanzania should not rely on gifts, loans or private foreign investment ('he who pays the piper calls the tune'): external money will not be enough, and dependence would endanger independence and socialism. It also says it is a mistake to put money and industries first, and that 'hard work' on the land is the foundation of development. He does not reject all aid: 'we are not saying that we shall not look for money from other countries'. A fair African-leader counterpart to Moyo's 2009 argument against aid, written 42 years earlier from a socialist standpoint; the two reach a similar conclusion for opposite reasons. The text records aims; the economic crisis and the 1986 IMF agreement are in the course from other sources.
